title: The 3-2-1 backup rule: why one copy is never enough
performance: the viewer checks where their important work files live and adds the missing copies so each is held as three copies, on two kinds of storage, one offsite

audience.assumed_prior: knows backups exist; assumes a file saved on the laptop, or synced, is safe
audience.why: corporate employees working from laptops; the brief names a non-technical audience
audience.motivation: not losing a deliverable or a week of work
audience.context: watched between tasks, with sound, at a desk; under two minutes

strategy.name: concrete_first
strategy.rationale: the rule is three bare numbers that only mean something when seen on one file facing real failures; each number answers one visible way the running example's report can be lost (F4, F5, F7, F8)
strategy.signature_move: show the report facing one failure, add the copy that survives it, then name the part of the rule that copy satisfied

misconceptions.belief: a file saved on my laptop, or a second copy kept on the same laptop or in the same bag, is safe
misconceptions.why_tempting: the file opens every day, and a second copy feels like a backup

misconceptions.belief: more copies is what makes data safe
misconceptions.why_tempting: the rule starts with a count, three
misconceptions.source_anchor: knowledge not_claimed: copies that can fail together add little; F6, F7

hook.sketch: Say your report is due tomorrow and lives in one place, your laptop. Tonight the drive stops working.

arc.promise: one rule of three numbers makes that night survivable, and you can check your own files against it
arc.bridge_from_prior: sec1 starts from what the viewer already does: saving work to the laptop and trusting it

sections.goal: the viewer can explain why a single copy of a file is a single point of failure
sections.carrier: the report on one laptop, the drive failing

sections.goal: the viewer can use the 3-2-1 rule to place three copies of a file: the original plus two backups, on two kinds of storage, one offsite
sections.carrier: the report copied to a second device and to the cloud, each copy surviving a different failure

sections.goal: the viewer can diagnose which part of the rule a given setup breaks
sections.carrier: a check: a laptop and a USB drive in the same bag, then the opening failure replayed and survived

arc.payoff: the same drive fails the night before; the report opens from the second device or the cloud, because the copies could not all fail together

practice_ladder.what: each copy of the report added in answer to a named failure, narrated
the viewer names the broken part of the rule for the same-bag setup before the narrator does
the viewer checks their own three most important files against the rule

slowdown_at: one offsite: copies in one place fail together

recall_moments.prompt_sketch: A laptop and a USB drive carried in the same bag: which part of 3-2-1 does it break?
recall_moments.answer: the one offsite copy: both copies share one place, so one theft or loss takes both
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: 'it is fine, there are two kinds of storage and a backup': true, but they travel together (F7, F8)

transfer_tasks: list where your three most important work files live today and name which part of 3-2-1 each one is missing

persona.voice: a capable colleague who has watched someone lose a week of work: calm, practical, a little dry
persona.delivery_notes: slower on each of the three numbers as it is named; a short pause after the check question; brisk on the payoff

gagne.attention: hook: the report's only copy, the drive fails
gagne.objective: promise: check your own files against one rule
gagne.recall_prior: sec1 starts from saving to the laptop
gagne.present: sec2 adds copies one failure at a time
gagne.feedback: the answer explains why 'two kinds of storage' is not enough there
gagne.transfer: transfer task: your own three files

merrill.problem_centered: the report at risk is the running problem
merrill.activation: sec1 from the everyday habit of saving locally
merrill.demonstration: sec2 shows each copy surviving its failure before naming the rule's part
merrill.integration: payoff replays the failure; transfer task hands the check over

mayer.coherence: one file, one laptop, one running example; no side stories
mayer.signalling: each number shown large as it is named; one slowdown on offsite
mayer.redundancy: labels only on screen, narration explains
mayer.contiguity: each copy appears as it is spoken
mayer.segmenting: three short sections, one idea each
mayer.pre_training: sec1 names single point of failure before the rule

arcs.confidence: one rule, three numbers, each seen working
arcs.satisfaction: the payoff: the same failure, survived
